h1: The 7 Best Jobsite Table Saws in 2026
description: The DEWALT DWE7491RS is the best jobsite table saw for most buyers, with a 32-1/2 inch rip and rack-and-pinion fence; 7 picks, including SawStop for safety.
dek: The DEWALT DWE7491RS is the best jobsite table saw for most buyers, with a 32-1/2 inch rip and rack-and-pinion fence; 7 picks, including SawStop for safety.
intro: A good portable table saw rips straight, stays square and keeps your hands safe. Here are seven worth buying, what actually separates them, and how to power one on a job site.

Every jobsite table saw cuts wood. What separates the good ones is the fence, because a fence that does not stay parallel to the blade causes both inaccurate cuts and kickback. After that come rip capacity, the stand and, for some buyers, a flesh-sensing brake that turns a life-changing injury into a bandage. Price matters less than you would think once you get those right.

sections.h: What Actually Matters in a Jobsite Table Saw

blocks.p: A jobsite table saw is a compromise by design. It has to be light enough to carry or roll onto a site, but accurate enough to rip plywood and trim stock cleanly. The best ones get there by spending their money in the right places: a fence that locks parallel to the blade, a stiff table and arbor, and a stand that sets up quickly. The worst ones spend it on features that look good on the box and leave the fence as an afterthought.

Almost every portable table saw in this class uses a 10-inch blade, a 15-amp universal motor and a no-load speed in the high thousands of rpm. That means the motors are broadly comparable, and power is rarely the deciding factor. A sharp, appropriate blade makes more difference to cut quality and to how hard the motor works than the difference between brands. A thin-kerf 24-tooth rip blade is the single best upgrade for ripping thick stock on a 15-amp saw.

What separates them is the fence, the rip capacity, the stand, the dust collection and the safety system. Those are the sections of this guide, and they are the things to compare. A saw with a mediocre fence and a great stand is a worse tool than the reverse, because the fence determines whether every cut is square and whether the saw is likely to kick back.

If you are searching for a Delta 10 inch table saw, note that Delta’s current 10-inch saws, like the 36-725T2 contractor saw, are a different class of tool: heavier, with cast iron tables and larger footprints, intended to stay in a garage or shop. They are fine saws, but they are not designed to be loaded into a truck every morning. If the saw will never leave the shop, a contractor or cabinet saw may suit you better. If it will travel, stay in the jobsite category below.

Finally, think about the rest of the cutting setup. A jobsite table saw handles rips and sheet goods; crosscuts on long boards are faster and safer on a miter saw. If you are buying both, our [miter saw stand guide](/best-miter-saw-stand/) covers the stand side of that pairing.

Rip capacity is the maximum distance between the blade and the fence, and it decides what you can cut. The number many buyers fixate on is 24 inches, the width of half a 4x8 sheet of plywood. Because the blade removes a kerf, splitting a sheet exactly in half lengthwise needs a little more than 24 inches, and wider parts such as cabinet sides or 30-inch panels need more again. The DEWALT DWE7491RS lists 32-1/2 inches, the Metabo HPT C10RJ lists 35 inches, and the SawStop and Skil list 25-1/2 inches.

More capacity is not free. The fence rails have to extend further, which makes the saw longer or requires rails that telescope. That adds weight and moving parts. For most trim and cabinet work, 24 to 25 inches is plenty. For framers and builders who rip full sheets of subfloor or sheathing regularly, 30 inches or more saves cuts and a lot of awkward handling. Breaking down full sheets on a small saw is also a safety issue, which we cover below.

Fence quality matters more than capacity. A fence must lock exactly parallel to the blade, every time, without you checking both ends. If the far end of the fence toes in toward the blade, the stock pinches between the blade and the fence, and that is the classic setup for kickback. If it toes out, cuts come out tapered. Rack-and-pinion fences, which move both ends together on geared rails, are the best design for portable saws because they stay parallel through their full travel.

DEWALT, Metabo HPT and Skil all use rack-and-pinion fences on the saws in this guide, and owners consistently rate them as the most accurate type in the category. Bosch and SawStop use different designs that are also well regarded. Avoid saws where the fence locks only at the front, unless the fence is very stiff; a front-locking fence on a light tube rail flexes under side pressure.

Whatever the fence type, check it when the saw is new. Measure from the blade to the fence at the front and back of the blade with a combination square, and adjust the fence until the measurements match. Recheck after transport. Owners commonly report that a quick check every few weeks keeps a good fence true for years.

The table below summarizes the seven saws on the points that decide most purchases. Rip capacities are the manufacturers’ listed figures to the right of the blade; check the current listing, since specs occasionally change between revisions.

Read the table by your top priority. If it is safety, the SawStop stands alone. If it is ripping full sheets, the Metabo HPT or the DEWALT DWE7491RS. If it is moving the saw constantly, the Bosch stand or one of the compact DEWALTs. If it is price, the Skil.

Prices range broadly. The Skil sits at the low end of the range, the DEWALT, Bosch and Metabo HPT sit in the middle, and the SawStop costs considerably more than any of them. The cordless DEWALT is moderately priced as a bare tool, but the batteries can make it one of the most expensive options if you are starting from nothing.

sections.h: Blade Guards, Riving Knives and Kickback

blocks.p: Kickback is the table saw injury most people do not see coming. It happens when the back of the blade, which is rising toward you, catches the workpiece and throws it back at high speed. The usual causes are a fence that is not parallel, a board that pinches the blade as internal stresses release, or a cut where the piece is trapped between the blade and the fence. The board can hit you hard, and worse, the hand pushing it can be pulled toward the blade.

A riving knife is the most effective defense, and every saw in this guide has one. It is a curved steel plate mounted just behind the blade that rises and falls with it, keeping the kerf open so the wood cannot close on the back of the blade. Leave it on for every through cut. The only time to remove it is for non-through cuts like dadoes, where the blade does not cut all the way through the board, and that is not something most jobsite work requires.

The blade guard and anti-kickback pawls are the other parts of the system. The guard covers the top of the blade and keeps fingers out of it. The pawls are toothed arms that dig into the board if it starts moving backward. Owners often remove guards because they get in the way of seeing the cut, and that is how many injuries happen. Modern modular guards come off and go back on in seconds, so there is no good reason to leave them off.

Technique matters as much as hardware. Use a push stick or push block for any rip narrower than about 6 inches, keep your hands out of the blade’s path, and stand slightly to the side of the blade rather than directly behind it. Never cut freehand without the fence or a miter gauge, and never use the fence and the miter gauge together for a crosscut, because the offcut gets trapped and kicks back. Support long and wide stock with outfeed and side supports so it does not tip off the table.

Breaking down full sheets of plywood on a portable saw is where many of these rules collide. A 4x8 sheet is heavy and hard to keep against the fence. Many pros cut sheets to rough size with a circular saw or track saw first and use the table saw for the final rip, which is both safer and more accurate.

sections.h: Flesh-Sensing Technology: Is SawStop Worth It?

blocks.p: SawStop’s technology works by putting a small electrical signal on the blade. Wood is a poor conductor and does not change the signal much; skin does. When the saw detects contact, it fires an aluminum brake into the blade, stopping it almost instantly, and the blade’s momentum drops it below the table. The result is typically a nick rather than a lost finger. SawStop has long published accounts of saves, and owners who have triggered it are among the brand’s loudest advocates.

There are costs. Each activation destroys the brake cartridge and usually the blade, both of which must be replaced. Cutting wet lumber, green wood or conductive material like some foil-faced foams can trigger the brake, so the saw has a bypass mode for those cuts, and you have to remember to turn it back on. The saw itself costs far more than any other jobsite saw in this guide. None of that changes the basic math for most people: the cost of a cartridge is trivial next to the cost of a hand injury.

Who should buy one? Anyone new to table saws, any shop where several people share the saw, schools and training programs, and anyone who has had a close call and does not want another. Experienced users who work carefully with guards and riving knives in place can reasonably choose a conventional saw, but the margin for error is much smaller. If the price is the only thing holding you back, it is worth stretching for.

Flesh-sensing is not a substitute for good technique. It protects against blade contact; it does not prevent kickback, which can still throw a board into your body. Use the riving knife, guard and push sticks on a SawStop exactly as you would on any other saw.

Jobsite table saws come with three kinds of stand, and the stand affects how you use the saw almost as much as the saw does. Rolling stands, like those on the DEWALT DWE7491RS and SawStop, have wheels and fold with the saw attached, so you tip it back and roll it like a hand truck. Gravity-rise stands, like Bosch’s, are a refined version that lifts the saw into position with one motion. Folding stands, like those on the Metabo HPT and Skil, have legs but no wheels, so you carry the whole assembly.

Rolling stands make the most sense if you move the saw often or work alone. They add weight, often a lot of it, but you rarely lift the whole thing. Folding stands are lighter and cheaper, but you carry the full weight of the saw every time it moves. Compact saws like the DWE7485 and DCS7485 sell the stand separately, which gives you the option of setting them on a bench or tailgate instead.

Dust collection is the weak spot of nearly every portable table saw. Most have a dust port under the blade and some form of guard-mounted port, and a shop vacuum connected to them catches a good share of the dust, but not all of it. The SawStop has a reputation for better collection than most, but none of these saws collect like a cabinet saw with a proper dust collector. Our [shop vac guide](/best-shop-vac/) covers vacuums and hose adapters that fit common saw ports.

Indoors, wear a dust mask or respirator rated for fine dust, especially when cutting MDF, which produces very fine particles. Outdoors, position the saw so the wind carries the dust away from you and from anyone else working nearby. Clean the saw’s internals periodically, because sawdust packed around the motor and the arbor causes overheating and binding over time.

sections.h: 15-Amp Circuits, Extension Cords and Generator Sizing

blocks.p: Every corded saw in this guide uses a 15-amp motor, which means it can draw close to the full capacity of a standard 15-amp household circuit under load, and more for an instant at startup. On a 15-amp circuit shared with lights, a radio and a shop vacuum, the breaker is likely to trip. The ideal is a dedicated 20-amp circuit, which is common in garages and required in many places by code for certain outlets. If you are adding a circuit for a shop, have a licensed electrician do it and pull the permit your jurisdiction requires.

Extension cords matter more than people think. A long, thin cord drops voltage, which makes the motor work harder, run hotter and bog down in thick stock. For a 15-amp saw, use a 12-gauge cord, and keep it as short as practical; a 14-gauge cord is only acceptable for short runs. Avoid daisy-chaining cords or plugging into a power strip. On construction sites, OSHA requires ground-fault protection for temporary power, so plug into a GFCI-protected outlet or use a GFCI cord set.

Running a table saw on a generator is common on new construction, and it works if the generator is big enough. A 15-amp saw draws roughly 1,800 watts running, and the startup surge can be considerably higher for a moment. A generator with at least 3,500 running watts and a surge rating comfortably above that is a sensible minimum for a saw alone; add the shop vac, lights and any other tools on the same generator and size up from there. Soft-start saws like the Bosch reduce the surge and are easier on smaller generators. Our [generator for camping guide](/best-generator-for-camping/) covers inverter generators, though most jobsite users will want a larger unit than a camping generator.

Always run a generator outdoors, well away from doors, windows and vents, never in a garage, basement or enclosed space, even with the door open. Carbon monoxide from a generator can kill quickly and without warning. Plug tools into the generator’s own outlets with heavy-gauge cords, and never connect a generator to a building’s wiring without a properly installed transfer switch or interlock, which a licensed electrician should install. If you work on sites without power often, the cordless DEWALT DCS7485 avoids the generator question entirely for lighter cuts.

Finally, unplug the saw or remove the battery before changing blades, adjusting the riving knife or reaching into the cabinet to clear a jam. It is the simplest safety rule and the one most often skipped.

sections.h: Which Jobsite Table Saw to Buy

blocks.p: For most people, the DEWALT DWE7491RS is the best jobsite table saw. It has a rack-and-pinion fence that stays true, a 32-1/2 inch rip capacity that handles full sheets, a rolling stand and the full set of safety equipment. It is the safe default for contractors and serious DIYers alike, and the large owner base makes parts and accessories easy to find.

If safety is your priority, or the saw will be shared or used by beginners, buy the SawStop Jobsite Saw PRO and accept the higher price. If you set up and move the saw several times a day, the Bosch 4100XC-10’s gravity-rise stand and soft start make it the most pleasant saw to live with. If you rip a lot of sheet goods and do not mind carrying the saw, the Metabo HPT C10RJ gives you the most rip capacity for the money.

On a budget, the Skil TS6307-00 is the cheapest portable table saw we would recommend, mainly because of its rack-and-pinion fence. For trim carpenters and DIYers who value portability over depth of cut, the DEWALT DWE7485 compact saw is easier to carry and set up, and FLEXVOLT owners who work on sites without power should look at the cordless DCS7485.

Whichever you choose, budget for a good blade, a set of push sticks and a shop vacuum. Those three things make more difference to cut quality and safety than the gap between any two saws in this guide. And if you are still deciding which brand platform to buy into, our [Milwaukee vs DEWALT comparison](/milwaukee-vs-dewalt/) and [laser level guide](/best-laser-level/) help round out a jobsite kit.

mistakes: Removing the riving knife and guard

The riving knife is the main defense against kickback, and the guard keeps fingers away from the blade. Owners remove them because they obstruct the view, and that is how many injuries happen. Modern guards come off and go back on in seconds; leave them on for every through cut you make.
Trusting the fence without checking it

A fence that toes in toward the back of the blade pinches the stock and causes kickback. Measure from the blade to the fence at front and back with a square when the saw is new and after rough transport. Adjust until they match, and recheck every few weeks.
Running the saw on a thin extension cord

A long 16-gauge cord starves a 15-amp motor of voltage, so it bogs down, overheats and wears out early. Use a 12-gauge cord as short as practical, avoid daisy chains and power strips, and plug into a GFCI-protected outlet on job sites as OSHA requires.

A small inverter generator may run a table saw once it is spinning but trip on startup, especially with a vacuum on the same outlet. Size for at least 3,500 running watts with good surge headroom, consider a soft-start saw, and always run the generator outdoors, far from doors and windows.

Pushing a narrow rip through with your fingers puts your hand inches from the blade at the moment kickback is most likely. Use a push stick or push block for anything narrower than about 6 inches, keep your hands out of the blade path, and stand slightly to one side of the blade.
bottomLine: The best jobsite table saw is the one with a fence that stays parallel to the blade and enough rip capacity for the work you do. For most people that is the DEWALT DWE7491RS, with the SawStop Jobsite Saw PRO for anyone who puts safety first and the Bosch 4100XC-10 for anyone who moves the saw all day. Whatever you buy, keep the riving knife and guard on, use push sticks, give the saw a proper circuit and a heavy cord, and run any generator well outside. A good blade and good habits will do more for your cuts than any spec on the box.

faqs.q: What is the best jobsite table saw for most people?
faqs.a: The DEWALT DWE7491RS is the safest default. It combines a rack-and-pinion fence that stays parallel to the blade, a 32-1/2 inch rip capacity that handles full plywood sheets, a rolling stand and a full set of safety equipment. Buy the SawStop if safety is the priority, or the Bosch 4100XC-10 if you move the saw constantly.

faqs.q: How much rip capacity do I need?
faqs.a: For trim, shelving and most cabinet work, 24 to 25 inches is plenty. To rip a 4x8 sheet of plywood down the middle you need more than 24 inches, so builders who break down a lot of sheet goods should look at saws with 30 inches or more, like the DEWALT DWE7491RS or Metabo HPT C10RJ.

faqs.q: Is a SawStop really worth the price?
faqs.a: For beginners, shared shops and anyone who values their fingers above the price difference, yes. The flesh-sensing brake typically turns blade contact into a minor cut. Activations destroy a brake cartridge and usually a blade, which you must replace, and it does not prevent kickback, so technique and guards still matter on a SawStop.

faqs.q: Can I run a table saw on a 15-amp household circuit?
faqs.a: Yes, but it can trip the breaker under heavy load or if other things share the circuit. A dedicated 20-amp circuit is better. Use a 12-gauge extension cord, avoid power strips, and if you need a new circuit in a garage or shop, have a licensed electrician install it with the required permit.

faqs.q: What size generator do I need for a table saw?
faqs.a: A 15-amp table saw draws around 1,800 watts running and more at startup. A generator with at least 3,500 running watts and strong surge capacity is a sensible minimum for the saw alone; size up for vacuums and other tools. Soft-start saws help. Always run the generator outdoors, far from doors, windows and vents.

faqs.q: Is a Delta 10 inch table saw a jobsite saw?
faqs.a: Generally no. Delta’s current 10-inch saws, such as the 36-725T2, are contractor-style saws designed to stay in a shop. They are heavier with larger footprints and are not intended to be hauled to a site every day. For a saw that travels, choose a jobsite model like the DEWALT DWE7491RS or Bosch 4100XC-10.

faqs.q: Do I need a 10-inch saw, or is an 8-1/4 inch compact enough?
faqs.a: An 8-1/4 inch saw cuts less deep, but still handles 2x lumber, trim, shelving and plywood. If portability matters more than maximum depth of cut, a compact saw like the DEWALT DWE7485 is easier to carry and set up. For thick hardwoods and the biggest rip jobs, choose a 10-inch saw.
